review.headline: A dominant position thrown away by one greedy capture

sections.text: You played the Italian and got a comfortable game against an opponent rated higher than you. Black's 3...h6 and 4...a6? were slow, and 4.d4 followed by 5.dxe5?! won a pawn.
You then lost some of the edge. 6.Nc3?!, 7.Nd5? and 8.a3? all let Black back in, and 10.Qe2? gave up another half-pawn. But 9.b4! was a good response to 8...Nge7?, pushing the bishop away.
After the trades on e3, Black blundered with 12...Nxd5??, and you played 13.exd5!, a pawn fork of the knight on c6 and the bishop on e6. From there you won material steadily with 14.Bxd5 and 16.Bxc6.

By move 24 you were far ahead. Then 25.Qxh6?? undid everything, because it left your own king short of air and allowed 25...Rxe1#. The engine's 25.Rxe8+ was the winning move, a back rank blow that worked in your favour.

review.turning_point: 25.Qxh6?? turned a totally winning position into a loss by mate; 25.Rxe8+ was a back rank shot that kept everything under control.
review.focus: Before any capture in a won position, check your opponent's forcing replies. At move 25, 25...Rxe1# was the only thing that mattered, and 25.Rxe8+ ended the game on your terms.

sections.text: This was a Bishop's Opening game that went into an open Italian-style centre. After 4.d3 Nd4 5.Nxd4 exd4 you tried 6.c3?! and 7.Nxc3, a sensible gambit-style structure, but 8.Bd2? was a small slip when 8.Bxf7+ was the more accurate shot.
You stayed active with 9.O-O, 10.Re1 and then 11.d4 and 12.e5, opening the centre while Black was still behind in development. By 13.dxe5 Nd7 you were up to +3.6.
Then 14.Qb3?? threw most of that away, since 14.Qf3 was stronger. Your opponent answered with 14...Bxc3??, grabbing a knight but running into 15.Bxf7+!, a fork of the king and the rook on e8.

16.Bxe8?? was a slip too, since 16.Qxc3 simply took the bishop. But Black did not take advantage with 16...Bxd2 and played 16...Qxe8??, and 17.Qxc3! picked up the loose bishop and left you well ahead.

review.turning_point: 15.Bxf7+! was the key shot, because it forked king and rook after Black's 14...Bxc3. That swing turned an equal position into a winning one.
review.focus: Take the free piece first. At move 16, 16.Qxc3 kept everything protected, while 16.Bxe8?? let +4.8 shrink to +2.0.

review.focus: At move 26, with a forced mate on the board, spend your last seconds checking every check. Practise playing the first twenty moves faster so you have time for moments like 26...Rf2#.

review.focus: Before you play a quiet developing move like 16...Nd7, check which checks and captures it allows. 16...Kf7 would have dealt with the threats on e6 and kept you in the game.

sections.text: Your opponent answered 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 with 2...Qf6?, bringing the queen out early. You did exactly what a coach likes to see and developed with tempo by playing 3.Nc3!, which already put you at +1.5.
Black followed with 3...g5?, trying to defend by pushing pawns, and you punished it with 4.Nd5!, hitting the queen and forcing it to retreat. The knight on d5 became a monster in the centre.
Then came 5.Nxg5?!. It won a pawn, but the engine preferred 5.d4, which kept more control. It hardly mattered, because Black played 5...f6??, opening the king.
From here you finished cleanly. 6.Qh5+! forced the king to move, 7.Nf7+ attacked the queen, and 8.Nxd6+ won it outright. 9.Qe8# ended the game.

review.turning_point: 5...f6 gave you a forced win: 6.Qh5+ drove the king up the board and 7.Nf7+ set up 8.Nxd6+, winning the queen.
review.focus: The only small point is 5.Nxg5?!, which gave up part of your edge. When you are already well ahead after 4.Nd5, prefer solid development such as 5.d4 and keep every piece working.

review.headline: A gambit pawn-grab that unravelled after one queen move

sections.text: You opened with a gambit idea: 2.d4 d6 3.dxe5 and 4.exd6 won a clean extra pawn, and you developed sensibly with 5.Nf3, 6.Bd3 and 7.O-O. That is a good way to handle the Nimzowitsch-style setup.

Your opponent then played 8...g6, a real slip that took the evaluation to +2.0 for you. The most accurate reply was 9.Bg5, which would have pinned the knight on f6 to the queen. Instead 9.Bb5? let the edge shrink to +0.6, and 12.Bh6?! after the bishop trade on c6 was another small step away from your best plan.

The game turned at 13.Qd4??. That queen move allowed 13...Nxf3+, a fork of your queen, rook and king, and the evaluation dropped from +1.5 to -2.6. Your opponent missed it with 13...c5, which gave you a second chance, but 15.Kh1?? threw it away again.
After 16.Bg5? and 17.Qd4? you walked into a queen trade that left you worse, and 18...Bxe1 picked up your rook. From there the extra pressure on f2 was decisive.

review.turning_point: 13.Qd4 was the decisive error: it put the queen on a square where 13...Nxf3+ forked three of your pieces, turning a +1.5 position into a losing one.
review.focus: Before every queen move, list the opponent's checks and captures. At move 13, a quick look at 13...Nxf3+ would have steered you to 13.Nbd2 and kept your advantage.

5.Nxd4 exd4 6.d3 and then 6...Bd6?? was your mistake, since it allowed 7.e5, which would have forked the bishop on d6 and the knight on f6. The engine preferred 6...c6.
Luckily, White played 7.Qg4?? instead, which left the queen on a square the knight on f6 attacked. That lost to 7...Bxh2+ 8.Kxh2 Nxg4+, which won the queen for a bishop.
White resigned after 8...Nxg4+, and the result was a short win with a lot of luck.

review.turning_point: 7.Qg4?? left the queen undefended against 7...Bxh2+ 8.Kxh2 Nxg4+, moving the game from -3.1 to +6.7 for you.
review.focus: At 6...Bd6 you left your pieces open to 7.e5. Before developing, ask what pawn pushes your opponent has.
